We have set out in the Budget papers and, indeed, in the paper on the deficit which accompanied the April, 1983 Budget, our thinking on how, during the time ahead, we are going to have a gradual reduction in the level of deficit spending in Canada. But make no mistake about it, Mr, Speaker, this side of the House, this Party, is not going to cut back drastically on government spending in the way which our friends opposite seem to think is not only desirable but, apparently, in their view, is quite possible.

Perhaps that still remains his view. However, is he not also saying that in reducing the number of those public servants, he is going to reduce substantially, if he were in office, a vast array of government programs? What is he talking about? If we are spending approximately $90 billion a year, are we going to cut out the social programs of which Canadians are rightly proud and which, during the period of recession through which we have passed, provided a safety net for those who could not provide for themselves?
His desk mate told us that his Party would eliminate universality. Then his Leader said, no, they would not eliminate universality. Then his desk mate said, yes, they would, and the Leader said, no, they would not. So I am not quite sure where that Party is on the question of social spending in Canada. However, unless the Hon. Member opposite; if he were in office-which is most unlikely-were committed to a policy of cutting out major social program spending on universities, medicare or old age, there is no way, Mr. Speaker, that deficits in Canada can be reduced overnight by 50 per cent or something of that magnitude. They can be reduced in the way I have described at 10 per cent or so a year, which is substantially different from what is done in the United States, which has, as I have said, a structural deficit of a character and nature fundamentally different from that in Canada.

apparently the Minister of State for Finance, who should be one Minister in that Government who would observe that, is absolutely uncaring. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite is ill advised, I would have thought, to speak of hypocrisy when he brings forth the resolution today, not many months after he told us he would do exactly what this Government is doing and what the Minister of Finance is doing. Mr. Speaker, when listening to the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) I was reminded of a book by Kathleen Hough called How To Lie With Statistics. I suspect that these Members have developed a fine art of selecting statistics to suit their purposes. The Minister of State for Finance says we on this side are presumably of the Chicken Little variety, concerned that the sky is falling. Mr. Speaker, I suppose I must say that 1 feel badly that I had misplaced the place of the interview and the source-
That is how accurate you are.

-but the former Minister of Finance in the Conservative Government said that, by and large, he agreed with that Budget put forward by the present Minister of Finance. When you consider what was in that Budget, that is quite a statement. I suspect that what he said in the House today will come back to haunt him in future weeks.
I want to go back to the point being made by the motion we are debating today. By and large it is a condemnation of the Government's economic and fiscal policies. Consider that the Minister of State for Finance has indicated that we have very real, sustainable growth taking place today. Our economy is quite strong. I wonder how on earth he can say those things when he knows perfectly well that interest rates are once again going up in what is now, I believe, the fifth week in succession. Unemployment is again increasing substantially. Inflation is increasing month by month. The Canadian dollar is falling, and would probably fall more if the Bank of Canada were not intervening on an almost daily basis to purchase Canadian dollars in order to keep it at an artificial level. Corporate investment in Canada is falling in spite of what the Minister has indicated. The misery index is on the increase.
By and large one has to ask the question: How could anyone, with those general trends before them and listening to any serious economist or financial adviser, say that the economy of Canada is healthy? You have to wonder whether the Minister has travelled throughout the country and looked carefully at the forest industry of Canada. After looking carefully at the forest industry of Canada, could you really say we have a healthy economy? After examining the West Coast, East Coast or inland fishery and talking to the people involved in the fishing industry, could you say our economy is strong and growing substantially? After looking carefully at the mining industry which stretches from one end of the country to the other, how could the Minister say that that particular sector is strong? After visiting the farming communities of Canada from Nova Scotia to British Columbia and really talking to the people involved in the production of food in this country, how can the Minister of State for Finance stand in his place and say that that sector is strong?
I am reminded of a quote by Mr. Michael Walker of the Fraser Institute. Not long ago he was quoted in Vancouver as saying that the Canadian economy is going full tilt. Presumably he did not say in what direction it was going full tilt, Mr. Speaker. A senior adviser to the right of center of today's society is suggesting to us that the economy of Canada is going full tilt. On what evidence is he saying this? How can people say that? That was said in the Province of British Columbia where the Fraser Institute is located. In that province there is

The Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) corrects me. I stand corrected. It might be called a Social Credit Government but it is being advised by the Fraser Institute. It is employing ultra-conservative policies and is made up primarily of card carrying Conservatives. Don't be so silly.

I challenge Hon. Members in the House to oppose the position that I take when they have an opportunity to rise. The economy of British Columbia is literally on its knees. Under that particular regime and with those particular policies in place the economy cannot by definition become healthy in the months and years ahead. It is a devastating situation, Mr. Speaker. I listen day after day as my friends in the Conservative Party complain about the deficit. I share that complaint. By implication there is the suggestion that if a Conservative Government were in power in this country the deficit would automatically be reduced.
I use two examples. I look to the Conservative Government which is in place in the United States and see what it has done with its deficit. Has it done what it promised the people of the United States it would do? When President Reagan campaigned in the last presidential election he literally promised the people of the United States that he would reduce the deficit in that country. Has he? Of course not. The deficit is significantly increased today. All implications and indicators show that it will continue to increase for many years.
We do not have to look at the United States, Mr. Speaker. We can look at our own country, and in particular at the Province of Saskatchewan. Today the Province of Saskatchewan has a debt that is increasing. It has not always had that debt. It has not always been in a deficit situation. For decades under the New Democratic Party led by individuals such as Tommy Douglas, there was no debt. There was absolutely no deficit or debt year after year, decade after decade. However, as soon as the Conservative Government took over in the Province of Saskatchewan, they had deficits and debts.
That happened before.

Yes, that happened before under Liberal Governments. When the New Democratic Party took over power in the Province of Saskatchewan, there was a debt. It was committed to reducing that debt. Not only did it reduce it, it eliminated it. For decades there was no deficit or debt. However, as soon as the Conservative Government took over in that Province, there was a deficit.
Myths can be perpetuated in this House by people presenting so-called facts which are unsubstantiated, very selective and highly edited. No wonder the people of this country are somewhat confused. No wonder the people of this country wonder what on earth the Federal Government and some of the provincial Governments of the country are doing. For example, Mr. Speaker, the Budget that the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) referred to, a Budget which he supported, was a Budget which brought a substantial number of tax concessions to the corporate sector of Canada. The Minister of Finance indicated clearly at that time that with a number of tax concessions-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I should not be misquoted here. I never said I supported the Budget of April 1983. I said it had some general thrusts that I agreed with. I have not said I supported the Budget. In fact, I voted against the Budget. The hon. gentleman should not say I supported the Budget of last April.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member very much for that intervention. I appreciate the Hon. Member for St. John's West clarifying the point that he supported the general thrust and a number of the-
Some of the general thrusts.

-some of the general thrusts of that Budget, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps not in its entirety.
To continue with what I was saying before I was interrupted, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance told the people of Canada that we must have patience, must be prepared to sacrifice, and must be prepared to share the burden of this recovery. He promised us that giving huge concessions to the corporate sector of the country, and in some cases to the upper income earners, was in our best interest because those individuals who had tax concessions provided to them would take the extra money and invest it in the economy in new plants, new equipment and new economic activity. As a result, jobs would be created for the unemployed in Canada, and this would go on year after year. Only part of that proposal worked, Mr. Speaker. Indeed the corporations received a considerable number of tax concessions. As a matter of fact, the President of the Bank of Montreal, Mr. Mulholland, was quoted as suggesting in a speech, made I believe in the City of Toronto, that the corporate sector of Canada was awash in tax concessions. He was really saying that the money saved through tax concessions could not be wisely invested in new plants and new equipment because of the under-utilization which was taking place in manufacturing in industrial Canada.
The Minister of Finance told only half the story when he said that by giving these huge tax concessions eventually economic development would occur, jobs would be created and unemployment would decrease substantially. With unused capacity in the 60 per cent to 70 per cent range, that reinvestment was simply impossible. One is not criticizing the corporate sector for not investing in new plants when present plants are operating at only 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 70 per cent of
March 30, 1984

their capacity. One is not saying that one would necessarily do anything differently. The point is that that did not work.
The Minister of State for Finance is saying that they are going to continue to do what they have been doing because they feel it is the right thing. It is obvious that the present policies of the Government will not get the economy of Canada going as we would like to see it and as the people of Canada ought to see it. In comparison with countries around the world, many of them our economic competitors, Canada unquestionably has the greatest growth potential. Unquestionably we have more natural resources, energy resources and capital resources at our disposal. We have more expertise and more high-tech at our disposal. We have a population that is relatively well trained and well educated, although that is being threatened by the Government today. The only thing we lack, Mr. Speaker, is the political will to do the job.
Many people say it is difficult these days to have political will to do the job. I want to remind Hon. Members that we have seen Governments have political will and we have seen programs implemented relatively quickly. I will use the national energy policy as a case in point. The decision of the Government was to introduce a national energy policy, and within a matter of a very few months we had a national energy policy in place. I also recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) deciding that the country needed a bilingual policy. By the stroke of a pen, a policy was created and put into place overnight which has created a different Canada in relation to bilingual issues. Also with the stroke of a pen the Government of Canada decided that we should have a metric program in place. Indeed, within a very short period of time that program was launched and it has literally changed the measurement system of Canada. We have seen identifiable examples of where the political will is in place and there is no question action follows. There is a need now as never before for the Government of Canada to work co-operatively with provincial and regional governments, to work carefully with the industrial business and labour sectors in order to draft a co-operative economic international strategy.
What about our successful competitors? I think of some western European countries and countries such as Japan which have had an approach in place for some years and as a result are, by and large, much more competitive and productive than we are. People have some sense of where they are going. People have some sense of their country's destiny. People see where they fit in, whether they are corporate leaders, labour leaders, individuals or governments. People see where they fit into the overall strategy. But what if we do not have a strategy? Then we find many of our important corporate areas, and in some cases very strategically corporate areas, in trouble. In this case I refer to such corporations as Dome, Chrysler, Maislin, Massey-Ferguson, Canadair, de Havilland, Cooperative Implements, Consolidated Computers, White Farm Equipment, Pioneer Chain Saw, St. Anthony's Fisheries and Electrohome Limited. The list could go on and on. When major corporations get into financial difficulties, the best we

have been able to do is to come in with some rather simplistic bailouts. Some have worked, some have not. In a sense, by definition, lacking any over all comprehensive economic and financial strategy, these bailouts cannot work because these corporations are not being bailed out in any particular context. If we had a national strategy in which all of the players were agreeing and participating, then perhaps we could view these so-called bailout requirements in some context. We could say in some cases, yes, it makes sense for the federal Government to use taxpayers' money to keep companies afloat and to encourage them into a more productive areas. In others we may decide that, no, because of the obvious direction in which this country is moving all the participants agree that this particular bailout does not fit into the overall strategy.
In summary, I suppose I support the general thrust of this motion put forward by the Hon. Member for St. John's West. I believe the Government has misrepresented the people of Canada in introducing appropriate economic and financial policies. I believe that one of the major items required in order to develop a sustainable economic growth and recovery in Canada is an economic strategy in the development of which all of the participants play a role.

Mr. Speaker, I listened intently to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). I found his speech very enjoyable but somewhat lacking in concrete recommendations as to what he or his Party might do to save us from the economic ills that have been visited upon us by the Liberal Government. He came in at the very end and made the pitch that his Party has made on several past occasions, that there should be some kind of a national strategy, some kind of centralized economic plan for the whole country. I do not really want to ask the Hon. Member a question, but I want to comment on that view even though he did not outline what might be contained in that plan.
I think there are great dangers with that type of approach to life. Is that not how they organize things in the Soviet Union?
Try Japan.

What about the people who want to dissent? What if somebody does not want to fit into that plan? What if they do not want to take up their assignment in the salt mine, or the potash mine in Saskatchewan or wherever they are told to go by a socialist government? This is a great danger that I behold in this idea where there is someone at the pinnacle somewhere in Ottawa who assigns every manufacturer, every farmer, or every worker in Canada into his little slot according to this plan, Sir. I stand up to dissent. I think the people who want to go fishing should be able to fish in whatever lake or sea they want. I think that if we were to have that freedom of choice in Canada, which is rapidly disappearing, then a lot of our economic ills from which we now suffer would be solved. We should not be going farther down the road to centralized planning.

Mr. Speaker, I can say that that is probably the most ridiculous statement I have ever heard raised in the

House of Commons. I have heard what I consider ridiculous statements made in the House, but that one takes the prize by leaps and bounds. What I was suggesting was planning with all of the players involved. One sees this in countries such as Japan, Austria, Switzerland, West Germany-
In China.
In Czechoslovakia and Poland.

-in Belgium, Norway, and Denmark. When you hear arguments put forward such as that of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), it is no wonder that people have questioned the validity of this House. After an attempt to deliver what I thought was a suggestion for consideration to hear Members stand up and purposely and consciously ridicule that suggestion, knowing that that suggestion is in place in the most progressive economics in the world today, is to misrepresent, misinform, slant, and present a biased picture. It does a disservice to this House and to the institution of Parliament. As he made his statement, I will let that go for my own.

Mr. Speaker, one does not want to disturb the serenity and the capacity of thought of Members of the New Democratic Party. They have not had a new view or a new idea in at least twenty years. I want to test the Hon. Member now.
The Conference Board of Canada has just given its quarterly Canadian forecast. Mr. Maxwell, the chief economist, said when he released the forecast that the Keynesian theory that you can spend your way out of recession "simply is not working". We have surely seen the proof of that in the last couple of years. We have just ended a year with, I believe, a deficit of $31.6 billion. We have $29.5 billion deficit forecast for this year. We have had deficits in the last few years totalling in excess of $90 billion. We are spending, spending, spending. But we still have a bad recession, terrible unemployment, and all the other ill effects. I want to ask the Hon. Member a two-part question. First, does he agree with Mr. Maxwell? Has the New Democratic Party come to its sense? Is the New Democratic Party now ahead of the Liberal Party in realizing that this approach does not work? The whole system today is shagged up. Our whole economic system is wrecked with these government deficits and borrowings. That is why we do not have any real recovery. Would the Hon. Member agree with that?
Second, would he agree that one of the differences between the piteous state of the Canadian economy today, and the American economy which is booming ahead with real growth, with much better employment prospects, is its lower deficit? The American economy is ten times the size of ours, and its deficit is about 50 per cent lower than Canada's. We have had tax increases in Canada. This is in sharp contrast to the expansionary fiscal stance of the United States. We have increased taxes; the Americans have reduced taxes. The only reason the Americans have a deficit that is so large is that they have also increased defence spending. Would the Hon.
Member for Kamloops-Shuswap not agree that this accounts for the difference between the two economies?
However, would the Hon. Member first agree with Mr. Maxwell that you cannot simply spend your way out of recession anymore? Are not the last four or five years living proof of the bankrupt policies of the establishment opposite, which is now tottering on its last legs toward a final cataclysmic event when the election comes?

Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is much more complicated than the question put by the Hon. Member for St. John's West. I think he wants a glib response that no, one cannot spend one's way out of a recession.
I believe that the more sensible way to approach it is to suggest that one can invest one's way out of a recession. I believe that now is the time when we have to find ways and means for encouraging average Canadians to invest in our economy once again, to encourage the corporate sector to invest in the Canadian economy once again and also to invest in the public sector in terms of developing the necessary infrastructure that an economy such as ours requires. To do that does not always result in increased government spending.
For example, I know that the Hon. Member feels strongly about the bribes that the Government presently gives to some of the major oil companies for exploration purposes. They amount to many billions of dollars for the last number of years and into the future. I do not think any serious economist would suggest that those bribes are necessary to encourage our oil companies to explore off of our coasts and in our frontier areas. If we were to take some of that bribe money that is given to the oil companies and perhaps if we were to collect some of the taxes that are presently called deferred corporate taxes, we would have a substantial amount of money to invest in the infrastructure that a country like Canada must develop in order to get on with developing our economy. Just so there is no mistake in the Hon. Member's mind, by infrastructure I mean better port facilities, better transportation facilities and perhaps some assistance to small business and the farming sector of our country. That is how we will get our economy going again.

3.	To the knowledge of the Government, were there any sales, by Canadian firms, of either prison detection or offshore surveillance systems to the Chilean Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1. Canada maintains normal diplomatic relations with Chile and we also pursue normal commercial relations that will benefit Canadian producers and exporters.
2.	The sale of defence related equipment to foreign countries, including Chile, is governed by the Export and Import Permits Act. As a matter of policy, the Canadian Government does not permit the sale of defence related equipment to countries engaged in hostilities or where there is an imminent threat of hostilities, or to countries for which the export of arms is forbidden by United Nations embargo. Applications for permits to export defence equipment that might possibly be used against civilians are carefully scrutinized and would be rejected if it appeared that such a use were probable.
There is no list of restrictions. However, a complete list of all products for which export permits are required is published as the "Export Control List" in accordance with requirements of the Export and Import Permits Act.
3.	To our knowledge, since export permits are in general not required for detection equipment of the type normally used by prisons, only Sparton of Canada Ltd. has been involved in the
Order Paper Questions
sale of a detection system evidently intended for use in prisons in Chile. This sale was made to a private sector firm, not to the Chilean Government. Government officials have been informed by the company that most of the content of the system was supplied by its U.S. parent company, although parts of this system were assembled in Canada and the marketing was done by the Canadian subsidiary. The installation of the system was done by the Chilean prime contractor. No permits were required for export of this equipment and, therefore, the Government had no opportunity to comment on the appropriateness of the sale.
With reference to offshore surveillance systems to Chile, we understand that only at one point a Canadian company had identified an opportunity for such a system but the project has since been deferred. No application was made for an export permit.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens (for Mr. Crosbie):
That whereas the depreciating dollar and increasing unemployment, inflation and interest rates endanger economic recovery and undermine job creation through their damaging effects upon agriculture, small business and business investment, this House regrets the government's failure to include in its February 15th Budget, or to adopt at any subsequent date, policies to provide the necessary conditions for a reduction in interest rates and the strengthening of the Canadian dollar and calls for the immediate resignation of the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) apparently had something to say about the fact that I was not here to speak at two o'clock. I do not know where he is now. I guess he spoke and ran. If he is still around, he might come in and I will tell him where I was. I was to be at the Canadian Police College at twelve o'clock for graduation ceremonies. They had the eminent good sense to ask me to be the guest speaker. I was to introduce this motion, but I was not able to introduce it between twelve o'clock and 1 p.m. because of the bells, for whom the bell tolls, because the ding-dong Government over there has not solved the bell problem. I could not leave the ceremonies before I spoke there in order to rush back here for
March 30, 1984

two. Therefore, my good friend, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), substituted for me as our first speaker and, of course, did his usual fantastic job.
If that settles the mind of the Minister of State for Finance, let me deal with his speech. His speech illustrated the smugness with which this Government is adorned. He is full right to the mug with smug. How could he treat the economic situation of this country as cavalierly as he did today and as his Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has been doing is beyond me. That smugness was illustrated in the Budget of February 15, when the Minister of Finance said:
In my April Budget, my goal was to secure the recovery. That goal has also been met.
What goal has been met? What recovery? Where is it? It is not present for the 1,476,000 Canadians who are unemployed. Since that Budget was brought down, every economic commentator has remarked on the fact that the Budget was based on unrealistic assumptions and forecasts, particularly the assumption that we are going to have an unprecedented six consecutive years of sustained economic growth. This is what the Minister's Budget said. We will be lucky if we even have any sustained economic growth today.
What has happened since the Budget came down, the Budget he is so pleased with, the one he says has met his goal of recovery? What has happened since then? The Bank of Canada rate has gone up for each of the six weeks since that Budget, from 10 per cent to the current 10.78 per cent. Interest rates have gone up, the prime bank rate from 11 to 11.5 per cent. Mortgage rates have risen by another half per cent or more, depending on the term.
Interest rates have been rising and are likely to continue to rise because the Canadian dollar has been depreciating just about every day since the Budget was brought down, particularly as a response to the stupidity of the Minister in saying, as he said and as I remarked in the House before on March 6, that he was not spending his nights up worrying that the dollar is not at 81 cents. What an incredible statement. If the Minister of Finance of this country is not worrying about the state of the currency in this country, the state of its economy and the state of its interest rates, how can we expect anything but that the currency of this country will devalue and be treated with the contempt it has been treated with since he made that statement?
Not only that, for two consecutive months the inflation rate has been back up again. It was down to a year-over-year rate of 4.2 per cent last November. It was up in December, up again in January. It has been up for the last two consecutive months, January and February. The latest figure is 5.5 per cent. The underlying trend rate of inflation is back up again. Surely that has to worry everyone. Even at a time of low inflation, our interest rates stayed at a prime rate of 11 per cent and higher. The real interest rate that people are now looking for on their money has exceeded 6 per cent and 7 per cent.
If the inflation rate is going to go up again, where are interest rates going to go? What is the reason interest rates
Supply
have been staying up as they have despite the lower inflation rate? It is the fear of renewed inflation. In the last two months we have seen the reason for people to fear renewed inflation. Interest rates have gone up, the dollar is tending down and there have been other economic consequences. We have seen the lack of business investment and the like.
The Minister of Finance continues to pretend that all of those trends do not represent a danger to our economic growth. He continues to pretend that there is not need for a change in government economic policies despite all these facts. The Minister has been pretending all along that things are out of his control, that the Government control what is happening, that we are prisoners of the United States, lock-step with them, that no matter what we do in Canada, we have to follow what happens in the United States. That is his usual theme. Last Monday the Minister gave lie to that theme in this House when he said, as reported at page 2422 of Hansard:
We are monitoring the situation carefully. If need be, we will make the necessary adjustments.
What more need will we want to see?
In the meatime I see no reason to change the basic policy that we have been following.
If that statement meant anything, it meant the Government could take steps. The Minister said they are monitoring the situation, but they are satisfied that this is the right course, there is no reason to change the basic policy and no need to make these necessary adjustments. This Minister is satisfied that 1,476,000 Canadians should remain unemployed. That is what he said.
When the Minister is asked in this House about the unemployment figures, he tries to pretend that we are doing as well or better than the United States. He croaks of how we have had a large number of new entrants into the labour force. What malarkey! These are people who have been unemployed donkey's months, if not years, and they are coming back out to see if possibly there is a job. This is supposed to indicate a better situation in Canada.
The facts are entirely different. What are the facts? In August, 1983 there was an unemployment rate in the United States of 9.5 per cent. In Canada it was 11.6 per cent in August of last year. In February of this year, the unemployment rate in the United States was 7.8 per cent, a decline of 1.7 per cent. What is the situation in Canada? We have an unemployment rate of 11.3 per cent. The decline in our unemployment rate has been 0.3 per cent as compared to a decline in the United States of 1.7 per cent.
Do you know how many new entrants to the labour force there have been in the United States in those months, Mr. Speaker? There have been 576,000 new entrants to the labour force in the United States. How many have we had in Canada? Only 61,000. What do new entrants to the labour force have to do with this pitiful performance in Canada as compared to the performance in the United States? Nothing, Mr. Speaker, and less than nothing.

March 30, 1984
Supply
The number of unemployed in the country is up for the fourth month in a row. The rate of unemployment is up for the second month in a row. The number of people working full time is now 352,000 fewer than the pre-recession peak and 68,000 fewer than the number working when the Government came into office four years ago. The number of young people with jobs is now 346,000 fewer than the number who had jobs before the recession and 288,000 fewer than when the Government took office in March, 1980, four years ago. The effect on jobs of this Government entering office is that 68,000 fewer adults have jobs now than four years ago and 288,000 fewer young people have jobs now than four years ago.
We hear and see the Liberal leadership candidates, five of whom are Ministers of the Government, going around the country pretending that they have some new economic approaches. The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) has a new economic program, but we have not heard what it is. He wants the Government to clear out of the board rooms of the nation. He does not want to have government intervention any longer, yet he remains a member of the most interventionist Government in Canada's history. The leadership candidate who is not a member of the Government is attacking the deficit. The Minister of Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) is attacking the deficit, and every Liberal Minister of Finance in the last 12 years has attacked the deficit, yet not one of them lifted a finger to do anything about the deficit which they are now attacking. It is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker.
I have here a study called Hidden Unemployment which was done by the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto. It indicates that 2,019,000 Canadians were unemployed last year and not the the 1,448,000 that Statistics Canada showed. Why is this? It is because Statistics Canada does not take into account discouraged workers who have given up looking for work because they believe there are no jobs available in the current market in Canada. This is the situation which the Minister said did not need adjustment.
Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that the situation calls for some adjustment when there is an unemployment rate of 11.3 per cent, 1.5 million Canadians who cannot find work are looking for work and another half a million Canadians are no longer looking for work because they know there are no jobs for them? If the Minister has the ability to make adjustments to his policy, has the need not been proven for him to do so? The Minister is not even present today to give us his reasons for not doing so.
The Minister usually says that he is helpless because of the United States. When he gets up in the morning and changes his underwear, he should put on the stars and stripes. He should wrap himself in the American flag because, according to him, only the United States can do anything to help the world. As reported on page 2467 of Hansard of March 27, 1984, the Minister said:
We are part of the world economy-
-that is something new that we did not realize, I am sure. He went on:
-and we are also very much affected by events in the United States.
There is the old United States again. Every time the Minister hears the word "United States", he salutes. This is the same Minister who two years ago insulted the Americans. He went to the United States and told them that we are going to take over the energy field, we do not want foreign investment, we do not want United States investment. He went down there like a raging lion, Marc the lionhearted in New York. He was telling them what they could do with their foreign investments. He told them they could shove it, and not to Canada but elsewhere. Now he says every day that we are very much affected by events in the United States. This Marc is a different Marc Antony.
Again on page 2467 of Hansard of March 27, 1984, the Minister is reported as saying:
If there is a rise in interest rates in the United States, clearly we would not be able to keep our rates at levels lower than those in the United States over a prolonger period of time.
This is the helpless Marc, the hapless Marc. He is certainly hapless and helpless. Anyone who reads the record will see that the comments he made in the House this week and last are confused, contradictory and shifty. He is shifting all over the place and does not know where to turn. This is not the certain, sure, strong Marc the lionhearted we have heard about who is going to save the Government. He is evasive, elusive, lacking certainty, looking around for pity, piteous looking. Of course, he is always arrogant and imperious. When shown wrong, he always proclaims his rightness. One need simply read his replies as reported in Hansard for the last two weeks to see that the economic fate of the country is in the hands of a man who does not know what to do, who has given up, who has no solutions and who will muddle through. His policy is one of muddleheadedness and addle-patedness.
The Minister is almost as bas as the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). Never have I heard such shus-wap as I heard from the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap today. He spoke gibberish with not one solid economic thought. Members on that side of the House have not grown beyond Cambridge University in the 1920s. They have seen where the Keynesian policies taken to their extreme have brought the Liberal Government of Canada, but they cannot even come up with anything new. All they want is the same old thing, only more of it.
Statistics Canada reports that "Consumer demand will continue to be restrained in the short term by the steady slowing of wages and weak labour market conditions". Does the Minister do anything about that? No, apparently that does not indicate any need for action. The Conference Board of Canada says that there is a slowing in the pace of economic growth this year and there is a possibility of a recession in 1985. Does that cause the Minister to take any steps? No, there is still no need to take steps. The Conference Board indicates that it cannot see any improvement in the unemployment rate and predicts a steady rise in unemployment to as much as 12 per cent in 1985. Does that cause the Minister to change his basic policy? No, apparently he does not recognize that that is needed.
March 30, 1984

As I mentioned earlier, the Conference Board has indicated that this dismal economic outlook results largely from "the continued high level of interest rates, particularly when viewed in relation to the rate of inflation". Does that bother this Minister? No, the Minister is not bothered by interest rate increases. Why, we heard him say this week that he pooh-poohed the damage done by interest rate increases. I know you do not believe me, Mr. Speaker, so I will read from the portion of Hansard in which he pooh-poohed. He said, as reported on page 2550 of Hansard:
-I explained that in spite of the increase in interest rates in Canada and the United States during the last few weeks, we should not necessarily conclude this will have a negative impact on employment and the growth rate of the Canadian economy any more than it does on the U.S. economy.
He says that we should not necessarily conclude this or we should not necessarily conclude that. Is that somebody who is speaking for a Government? If interest rates will continue to rise, the only conclusion we can come to is that there will be no economic recovery. We have seen that interest rates of 11 per cent have stopped the recovery in its tracks. Will interest rates of 11.5 per cent be any better?
We should not necessarily conclude this, that and the other. I can necessarily conclude that the Minister does not have a grip on what is happening in the country. He has served us too long. He and the Government are tired and have no new vigour or ideas which will change economic policy. They should do what this resolution asks them to do. They should resign and go to the people of the country and let them make the judgment as to who should lead the country out of the economic morass into which they have led us.
Again on page 2550 of Hansard, the Minister is reported as saying:
The Government does not favour an increase in interest rates.
That is a fantastic statement, Mr. Speaker. When is it going to do something to stop the increase in interest rates? No one favours an increase in interest rates. What kind of malarkey is that for the Minister to give to the House of Commons when he is asked a question? He goes on to say, "We are living in the real world, we are on the North American continent-" He did not even know three years ago that we were in the real world or on the North American continent. He was going to throw the Yankees out. Today we know what he is doing with the Yankees and we know what he is kissing down in the United States of America.
He also said, "-the Canadian and U.S. economies are extremely interdependent". We are in the hands of economic mountebanks, Mr. Speaker. If we do not change them, God only knows what is going to happen to the people of this country and to our economic future.
Unfortunately, I do not have time to cover all the points I would like to as I have only 20 minutes. In his remarks in the House this week the Minister did not say that his February Budget was based on the assumption of lower interest rates. I do not have the time to quote him now, but those interested in
Supply
what he said about the Canadian economy in recovery should turn to page 15 of the Budget where he said:
Further progress in reducing interest rates and the growth of cost is essential if the business sector is to restore its Financial strength and become a sustaining force in the recovery.
That is what he said in the Budget, but this week in the House he told us not to worry about interest rates going up, that we cannot necessarily assume anything. Why then did he make that statement in his Budget on February 15 if it did not matter and if we cannot assume anything? In his Budget he went on to say:
Without a gradual return of real interest rates to more historic relationships, there is a risk that the medium-term real growth outlook for Canada and elsewhere will be weaker than projected.
You had better believe there is a risk, Mr. Speaker. There will be no medium growth in Canada if interest rates continue to go up.
The Minister does not have any powers of prediction either, Mr. Speaker. On October 19, 1983, he predicted that interest rates would drop by another two to three percentage points in the next six months. But they have gone up by a half percentage point, Mr. Speaker, not down two or three percentage points. Imagine the Minister of Finance making a prediction like that which turned out to be so wrong. On May 11 he said that interest rates were to stay stable. What does stable mean if it does not mean that they do not move at all? He said that interest rates would remain stable for most of 1984 and drop toward the end of the year. So much for anyone who believes any of the predictions made by the Minister of Finance.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to move on to one other egregious error, if it was not deliberate, of the Minister in this House this week. On Tuesday, March 27, as reported at page 2467 at Hansard, he said:
We need a lot of borrowing from abroad because we do not have enough resources in this country to ensure the full potential that this country has.
Then he went on to say-

Last Tuesday the Minister also said that we had a net capital inflow of $5.5 billion last year. The Minister continued, as reported at page 2468 of Hansard:
We had a net inflow into this country of $5.5 billion in foreign investment in 1983. My friend should look at both sides of the picture and realize that Canada has been a net beneficiary of foreign investment in 1983.
That is completely wrong, Mr. Speaker. I do not suppose it is deliberately wrong; the Minister is just confused, uncertain, shaken up. In 1983 in Canada the actual position with respect to what the Minister calls net capital inflow was that there was

$200 million of direct investment in Canada and Canadians invested $2,525 million abroad in the same year. There was no net capital inflow into Canada of $5.5 billion; there was a net flow out of direct investment of $2,525 million. Canadians are sending their money out of the country because they have no confidence in the Government. To that should be added $6.6 billion in unidentified outflows. We had an investment outflow of $8.9 billion, not a net foreign inflow into Canada of $5.5 billion. There was $2.3 billion in direct investment and $6.6 billion was unidentified. speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: In conclusion-

Mr. Speaker, I have unanimous consent so 1 have to finish making my point.
Imagine the Minister of Finance making such a gigantic error when answering questions in the House. He should tender his resignation on Monday, Mr. Speaker. The only time we have had a greater investment outflow than we had in 1983 was in 1981 with the National Energy Program of the same Minister, when he was Mr. Hyde, the big bully-boy of the international investment scene-Mr. Hyde, but today he is Dr. Jekyll. He has his other face on today as Minister of Finance. As a result of the NEP and FIRA, in 1981 we had investment outflows of $20.3 billion, including $11.3 billion in direct investment lost to this country. In 1981 we still lost money. Canadians and foreigners who had money invested here are moving it out of the country. If that were not the case, Mr. Speaker, why would there be pressure on the Canadian dollar when there is a positive trade balance and a positive balance on the current account?
I was given unanimous consent in order to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, so I will conclude by saying that all these points illustrate that the time has come for the Minister to admit that his policy is not succeeding. Since he has admitted that he can make adjustments, since he changed his tune last Monday, the time has come for these adjustments to be made. There are 1,476,000 reasons for adjustment to be made-they are the officially unemployed Canadians. There are another 600,000 reasons for adjustments to be made, and they are the unemployed Canadians who are not included in the statistics.
If the Government will not take this action, Mr. Speaker, then this resolution calls for it to resign. It has been in office for four years, and that has been four years of economic misery for the people of the country. It is time to put in another group that will take a different approach and will have the guts to do what they say must be done, and that is, to reverse the economic policies that are now under way, the sloth, the whole succession of deficits of the last 12 to 14 years, the inability to get up the gumption to attempt to tackle it.
It is time for the electorate to be given the chance to show if it wants a continuation of the last four years with the same group in government, perhaps with a different leader. We all know that the question is, "Would you buy a used government from that new leader, Mr. Turner, or not?" That is the
question that Canadians are going to be asked-"Would you buy a used Government from this man or would you want to try a Party that has been opposing these ruinous, wasteful economic policies of the last four or five years?" That is the Party that I represent, Mr. Speaker.
Thank you for giving me the time to conclude, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy the comments of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I have a two-part question for him. It seems to me that when he was Minister of Finance he reappointed Governor Bouey to the Bank of Canada. Knowing Governor Bouey's record, it was perfectly clear where he stood in terms of monetary policy and how he viewed the high interest rate policy of the Government. Why did the Hon. Member reappoint Governor Bouey, knowing where he was coming from, to put it in popular parlance?
The Hon. Member criticized the Minister of Finance for having said that adjustments would be made if necessary. He made the case very well that adjustments are required today. Could he give us two or three ideas of what his adjustments would be if he were given the opportunity to make them?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for giving me the chance to address those questions. The Hon. Member should not make the silly mistake of blaming Governor Bouey for our present economic situation. It is only Governor Bouey who is standing between us and complete and utter economic disaster. Governor Bouey did not cause this situation. This situation is caused by the policies of this administration over the last ten years or 12 years. It so weakened our economy with its ever increasing deficit, with which we are all familiar, and its economic policies, that the only thing standing between Canada becoming a banana republic and economic chaos is Governor Bouey, who is trying to defend our currency. He is trying to operate in such a way that we will have a country which can still compete internationally and will not go through ruinous inflation again.
What would interest rates come to if we allowed the dollar to go down 10 cents or 15 cents, or whatever, and then went into another round of fantastic inflation? The whole cycle would start again. Where will the Canadian dollar end up? The Canadian dollar has been devalued, Mr. Speaker, in the last four years something like 22 per cent or 23 per cent. That has not been the solution. It has not brought economic miracles to Canada. Suppose the Canadian dollar devalues another 25 per cent? What can that do except to bring us quickly down the slope to economic chaos together with ruinous inflation. Do we want to be another Brazil with 250 per cent inflation, another Israel, or any of those countries which cannot keep up?
It is not Governor Bouey, it is the policies of the Government which got the Canadian economy, particularly on the fiscal side, in the shape it is in. It is not Mr. Bouey's fault. If Mr. Bouey was not there, we would have to invite another "Bouey". So do not worry about Mr. Bouey. It is the Govern-
March 30, 1984

ment which is responsible for this wreckage, not Governor Bouey. He is a consequence of the policies of the Government.
With regard to the second point, what would I do? First, I will say that nothing can save the economy while this Government is in power. No one has any confidence in it. Capital is going to flee this country because of its record of intervention and incompetence. If we are there, confidence will be restored; the flight of capital out of Canada will stop; the pressure on the Canadian dollar will stop. One thing I would not have done is to bring in the tax increases which the Minister of Finance brought in in April and which he confirmed again in February. How could this be the right time to have tax increases when there is not any kind of vigorous recovery going on in the economy? I would not impose another 1 per cent increase in the sales tax on the Canadian people in October, and I would not have made the changes in the child tax credit and the other changes which were introduced in the Budget of last April. So we would not be going on this course.
Why is the United States doing better? Because despite its budget deficit, which is considerably less than ours, it has reduced taxes. It has not gone, like the Minister of Finance and the Government of this House, in the other direction. The record of Mr. Reagan is fantastically successful compared to the Trudeau-Lalonde record. Reagan streaks ahead of them economically. The U.S. has 7.8 per cent unemployment. Here we have everybody unemployed. Mr. Trudeau started with 360,000 Canadians unemployed. Today he has 1,476,000.

Mr. Speaker, I have a certain amount of respect for the hon. gentleman who just spoke. I believe his feet are on the ground. He is certainly not like his Leader, who probably gets up every morning and looks in the mirror and takes a bow. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman, if he is advocating an increase in the value of the dollar, whether he would like to make that policy statement on a wharfhead of a fish plant in the City of St. John's? I would like to ask him if he believes he would survive being hove off that wharf into the water? And if there are any ice pans there, he would be tabby-panning across to the south side hills.
Would the Hon. Member state clearly now whether it is the policy of the Progressive Conservative Party to bring up the value of the Canadian dollar, and how far, and would he admit it to the fish processors in Newfoundland and the fishermen, who do not receive enough in unemployment insurance benefits?

Well, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is getting all exercised about this Government's policy. That is exactly the policy of the present administration. Does he not realize that the Government permitted interest rates to go up
Supply
just so that the value of the dollar would be increased? When the hon. gentleman goes back to see his fishermen, would he advise those fishermen that his Government has just prevented the dollar from sinking down to 75 cents, 70 cents, 60 cents or whatever he thinks they want it to sink down to? Because when the fishermen realize that, they will throw the Hon. Member over the head of the wharf on his keester. When they realize that this Government has kept interest rates high and allowed them to go up to 22 per cent a year and a half ago just to protect the dollar, the hon. gentleman will not even get to the wharf. They will have him cooped up in a barrel and capsized before he even gets to the head of the wharf.
Yes, we do not stand for a deliberate devaluation of the Canadian dollar. No country can prosper which deliberately allows its currency to devalue. I will say that to the fishermen on the wharf in St. John's West, or anywhere else in Newfoundland. I will defend my economic policies. In fact, their love for me is shown by the fact that my vote increased fantastically down in St. John's West after my last Budget. When they give me a chance to bring in another one, it will be 100 per cent down there.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy the spectacle of a speech by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), because that is what it is, really, a spectacle. No wonder he receives a lot of invitations to speak across the country. He is a big drawing card. He makes people laugh and is good on his feet. When people are in an atmosphere where they want buffoonery, the best guest they can get is the Hon. Member for St. John's West. As a matter of fact, sometimes I think I would invite him to come to my constituency, because he would draw a lot of people.
This man, who ran in the leadership convention last year, did very well. I was proud as a Canadian to see that he did so well. Some people say that had it not been for having to speak French or understand French, perhaps he would have become leader of the Conservative Party and perhaps he would have become Prime Minister of the country. As a Canadian who is a francophone and happens to be from Atlantic Canada, I felt some sympathy for the Hon. Member because, really, a person should not be deprived of gaining power because he does not speak one or the other language. However, what the Hon. Member should realize is that the fact he could not speak French did not really hurt him that much in the convention, because I feel that unilingual francophones who cannot understand English would have probably voted for him if they had not understood what he said.

speechtext: Order. Could I invite the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) to speak to today's motion, please?
Good idea.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, unilingual francophones, listening to the Hon. Member speaking on his

March 30, 1984

motion today, would be more likely to agree with him if they did not understand what he said. If they had understood what he said last June, then he would have lost some delegates in the convention. No question about it.
What the Hon. Member is talking about is supply side economics. I applauded a while ago when the Hon. Member said that President Reagan had a great policy. I was happy to hear the Hon. Member for St. John's West tell the House of Commons and the public that that is what he wants, supply side economics.
That is the kind of policy which President Reagan has brought to the United States of America. The Hon. Member for St. John's West is really an honest man. He has been saying it in public since he has been finance critic of his Party, only to be repudiated by his Leader, who has a hidden agenda. He says the truth. He says it and he means it. He says he admires the economic policies of the U.S. and their job-creation record. He admires the way they have brought down inflation and unemployment. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there are ways to create jobs and bring down inflation other than the way this Party and this Government has done over the past 16 years or so. You can stop the economy flat. You can do what President Reagan and the Hon. Member for St. John's West say is great. You can cut off welfare payments to people, you can cut off food stamps for people at the low end of the economic scale as they did in the U.S., and increase military expenditures.
President Reagan is not running a tight fiscal ship. He has increased military expenditures to an incredible level and reduced the expenditures affecting low-income people, the poor. That is what he has done. That is not running a tight fiscal ship. The Hon. Member says he loves this because he is talking supply side economics. He says that if you look after the wealthy, the powerful, the big institutions and large corporations, the benefits will trickle down to the people. But they do not, Mr. Speaker.
The Liberal approach is to reject supply side economics because it increases the economic and social gaps in society. We have another way to go about it.
The Hon. Member also spoke about the National Energy Program and this Government's foreign investment policy. I wonder if he realizes where he is from. He is from Newfoundland. The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) asked him about the strength of the Canadian dollar. The motion of the Hon. Member for St. John's West says:
That whereas the depreciating dollar ... undermine job creation through their damaging effects upon agriculture, small business and business investment-
Well, the Hon. Member, in his answer to the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, said that yes, he wants to strengthen and increase the value of the Canadian dollar. But the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate rightly pointed out that the fishermen in St. John's West or in his riding, or in northeastern New Brunswick, cannot sell their fish, or the company to which they sell fish cannot resell it, unless they undercut the European countries which are dumping fish in the U.S.
because they have devalued their currency. How can a Member from Atlantic Canada, in this economic context, be sincere to the people he represents if he advocates an increased value in the Canadian dollar? That will ruin the Atlantic fishery. The pulp and paper industry in Atlantic Canada, in fact all over Canada, is having a hard time because we have to compete with European economies which have devalued their currencies. When the value of the Canadian dollar, Mr. Speaker, is reduced by market forces, not by deliberate Government policy, what happens? The regions of this country which export products which were protected by the national economic infrastructure and trade policies this Government has built up, in other words Ontario and parts of Quebec, are the ones that benefit.
If the country accepted the economic and monetary policy of the Hon. Member for St. John's West, we would not let the market determine the value of the dollar. He would want to increase it. The result is that the Atlantic fishery could not compete, the pulp and paper industry and construction industry could not compete.
The Hon. Member criticized the NEP and said it was a bad policy because some American interests did not like it. Does he not realize that it is because of the NEP that billions of dollars are being invested now in the Newfoundland offshore? The NEP rationale was to say that now that we have obtained just about the limits of new discovery of oil from conventional sources, there are still secondary discoveries and tertiary recovery methods. Over the last 30 odd years a tax and price regime was put in place to permit Alberta and Saskatchewan in particular to develop a petroleum industry. The rationale of the NEP is that now we have to look elsewhere, we have to look at the so-called Canada Lands because they are under federal control. The offshore is federally controlled, as the Supreme Court of Canada confirmed two weeks ago. We said we now need a new regime. Who but the Parliament of Canada can provide that regime?
The NEP, Mr. Speaker, is there to make sure that in the Canadian north, in the Atlantic offshore, we will have a regime which will encourage exploration for oil and gas. Therefore, I just do not understand how a Member from Atlantic Canada can suggest that the NEP has been bad for the country.
A lot has been said about the deficit and how it is supposed to be so bad. But, Mr. Speaker, why do we have a deficit in Canada, and how can we deal with it? We have a deficit because, first of all, in the mid-1970s the Government started to change the tax system so as to leave more money in the hands of Canadians in order to stimulate the economy. In order to make the tax system more equitable, we adopted a proposal that the-the former Whip of the official Opposition laughs at that. It was advanced by one of his former Leaders to make sure that the federal Government would not benefit from inflation. Indexed personal exemptions meant that less revenue came into the federal Treasury.

You did not cut expenditures.
March 30, 1984

That is right, because we also indexed the social payments to the cost of living. The result is that more money goes out and less money comes in. So you have a deficit. Then, later in the 1970s, we had the oil crisis. The federal Government determined through a series of policies that we would have a tax regime and the National Energy Program to give incentives to develop the petroleum and gas industry. We had policies to help people insulate their homes and reduce the consumption of oil for the good of the whole country. We wanted security of supply. That means you use the fiscal policies of the Government of Canada. You increase expenditures, but you do not necessarily increase revenue when you do that. The revenue has not come in because world petroleum prices have not continued upwards. Therefore, we cannot sell our natural gas in the U.S. as we thought we could because we have to be competitive.
Another reason for the deficit is that in the last two years we have had a recession. Now you need to be mischievous or not understand anything about the economy to suggest that the recession we just came out of had its roots in Canada. How can anyone, unless he is being overly partisan, suggest that Canada was the only country that had a recession? The causes of the recession were partly in Canada, but they were in greater part from outside of Canada. The economy was stopped dead in the United States through monetary policy because President Reagan agreed with the Chairman of the Federal Reserves Board in the United States to recoup a great part of the American dollars which were financing the rest of the world for so long. They did that by increasing interest rates. What should countries which border on the United States do? Should they close their eyes and ignore what happens in the United States? That is done at a great cost. We determined we could not do that. That had the effect of slowing down the Canadian economy because people were worried about high interest rates. They were not building homes, buying cars or buying appliances. Therefore, unemployment was created.
To suggest that the economic recession which we just went through had its causes only in Canada is not to understand the workings of the economy of Canada, let alone of the rest of the world. During that recession we did not cut down on social programs as they did in other economies such as Great Britain and the United States. We continued to increase them. This is the basic difference between supply side economics and Liberal economics, between the Tories and the Liberals. We did not reduce social expenditures for people who cannot defend themselves, the real victims of an economic recession. We did not cut back on UIC payments. We increased them. We did not cut back on our payments to provinces for medicare, postsecondary education and equalization. The poorer provinces of the country continued to get increases from the federal Treasury. When the recession was at its worst and the federal deficit was going up, we were still increasing payments to Newfoundland, P.E.I., New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Manitoba by over 12 per cent a year. Even when we had a restraint program to limit discretionary expenditures of the
Supply
federal Government to 6 and 5 per cent, we continued to increase health transfers to provinces by 13 per cent. We transferred post-secondary education to 6 per cent but we did not touch the equalization program. In my Province of New Brunswick it went up by 11 per cent from 1982-83 to 1983-84.
Liberal Governments do not adopt policies that only protect the economy for the wealthy, the powerful and those who can look after themselves. We do it more gradually because the economy will correct itself gradually. In the meantime, with a series of safety mets, we protect those in society who cannot protect themselves from the ravages of inflation, unemployment and economic recession. That is why we have a high deficit.
Is the deficit too high? That is a question of judgement. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that in the mid-term the deficit will come down. It is now about 8 per cent of the GNP. It will go down to about 4.7 per cent in the fiscal year 1987-88. The financial requirements of the Government will go down from 6.9 per cent of the GNP to 3.4 per cent of the GNP in three years.
When Canada participated in World War II, our deficit went up to over 20 per cent of the GNP. Did the economy stop flat? After the war we had an incredible period of growth. Saying that the deficit automatically means we are not going to have economic recovery, that the economy is going to be stifled because of the deficit, is all hogwash. Some of our partners in the OECD have higher deficits. Japan has a higher deficit than that year after year. In Japan they have such a high trade surplus that they have a surplus of yen. They absorb it with high fiscal deficits. With the savings rate at over 14 per cent of personal disposable income in Canada today, if we did not absorb a good part of that savings rate at the federal and provincial levels, chances are we would have to export finance and invest money elsewhere. The Japanese had to invest yen outside of their country. That is not necessarily bad because it builds relationships with partners.
The federal Government has a high deficit not only because it refuses to balance its books. It is because the federal Government has a fiscal responsibility in the overall economy. It has a responsibility to make sure that the ups and downs are as smooth as possible. In private industry, private budgets and even in provincial governments it is possible to balance the books. However, over and above the expenditures and revenues we must look at the overall economic interest of the country in the mid-term and in the long term. We must use the credit of the whole country to the advantage of the overall economy. With government expenditures we must make sure that an economic recession will not hit only those who cannot defend themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member for Burlington has a lot of useful information to give us so I will try to be as brief as possible. The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) and the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), who just spoke, seem to be supporting the NDP policy of allowing the Canadian dollar to sink lower and lower.

March 30, 1984
Supply
They say that will encourage trade. That might be so. However, it does that because in real terms the value of wages and salaries in Canada will decline. On this side we want to encourage additional trade, but we would do it by encouraging productivity, making each unit of effort produce more.
Why does the Government advocate a decrease in wages and salaries for Canadians in the country?

Mr. Speaker, neither I nor the Member for Gander-Twillingate said that we encouraged a policy to decrease the value of the Canadian dollar, or sink the Canadian dollar, as the Member just said. No one ever said that here this afternoon. The Opposition says that is what we say. However, that is not what we say. We say that the dollar should reflect the market forces, that it should be at the value the market forces dictate. It is true that a lower dollar improves your export opportunities, but it can damage you importwise. Over a period of time this has the effect of putting some pressure on wage rates and on all cost pressures. This is true in the manufacturing sector in particular, in the areas that are already strong. However, in the resource areas of the country; the west, the north and Atlantic Canada, that will not happen. If the Canadian dollar is too strong, we cannot sell our resources. Of course, there is a cost and an opportunity to everything. I agree that some sectors in the Canadian economy will feel the competitive forces of their wages at one point. I say it will be the stronger sector of the Canadian economy that will suffer. It will be those workers who already do very well who will suffer the competition. I do not mind that happening for the benefit of creating jobs in those regions of the country which benefit from exports where unemployment is always chronically higher.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There being no further questions or comments, we will proceed to debate. The Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling).

Mr. Speaker, I could not bring myself to ask any questions of the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). I looked up in the gallery and I noticed some people holding their mouths. I thought they were going to throw up. Perhaps it might be an idea to have sick sacks in the gallery to take care of people who cannot abide speeches such as the one the Hon. Member made on economics. I have never in my life in all the time I have been here listened to such economic gibberish as I heard from him. I do not think he could run a hot dog stand and lose money. He is just a disaster.
There is not much time left this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. I might say that much has been said about the Budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on February 15. Some say it should have this measure or that measure of relief, or some favoured provision that has been promoted by a lobby. But the reality is that it is not just the February 15 Budget that is at the root of our problems. It is really the last four Budgets. The damage done by the three previous Budgets could not be reversed in the last Budget because governments
do not advertise their mistakes or admit to errors in judgement. This is evident from the twisted and tangled rhetoric of the Member who just spoke. Clearly what we need is a period of stability to allow many of our businesses to restructure their finances. They simply cannot expand and employ more people, raise the GNP and help reduce the deficit if they are debt-financed. That is the problem being faced.
Many businesses are operating with a sizeable loss carried forward. This was recognized to some extent in the Budget and the carryforward term was extended to seven years. But if you think about it for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, a profit applied against a loss carried forward means that that business will pay no taxes to the federal Treasury, or at least it will pay very much reduced taxes. It means that government expenditures must be cut to accommodate the shortfall in revenue, or taxes must be raised in other areas to pick up the revenue shortfall, or additional borrowing must be made. We can see what has happened here. The Government is using a combination of the last two: borrowing more money and in some areas raising taxes.
Clearly some measures to increase and encourage equity investment beyond that which is presently in place must form part of the strategy for any budget.
Many of us thought we would have seen such a provision in the last Budget. Some even speculated that there would be a flow-through feature of losses carried forward to other income. That feature could have repaired the capital accounts of many businesses if, say, 50 per cent of the flow-through benefit were required to be reinvested in businesses. Some people may have difficulty in following that thought but, in simple terms, many businesses have been stung by high interest rates and are reluctant to finance an expansion program on borrowed funds, especially in a volatile money market.
Somehow we must break out of the mould into which the last four disastrous Budgets have cast us. Let us say you operate a small to medium sized business, Mr. Speaker, and you want to expand to capture a larger market outside of Canada. Say you need new productive machinery to enhance your gross profit but you are reluctant to place the order because you must borrow the money on a term loan with a floating rate. You look at your cash flow for a period ahead and you are aware that the capital cost allowance for the first year on that new piece of machinery will be 50 per cent of what it was two years ago. You find yourself having to seek a larger line of credit at the bank with a floating rate in a volatile money market. There, in simplified terms, lies the dilemma facing many business people in Canada who are being urged by the Government to venture and increase markets, and to expand employment, to add more people to the payroll and reduce unemployment.
It is obvious to anyone who thinks seriously about business that the only way you can undertake new markets, purchase new productive machinery and hire new people is by finding new sources of equity. An equally important problem is that so many governments and business gurus worship at the high technology altar, and the Government's actions to encourage equity investments are directed almost exclusively at high-
March 30, 1984

tech. What it does not realize is that even at the turn of the century the bulk of the people employed in this country will be employed in low technology industries. We have to have a window on the world, and high technology certainly has a place in our economy. Anyone would be foolish not to acknowledge that. But it is not the end-all to everything, and that we have to recognize. Some investors will not look at you if you do not say magic words such as robot, transistor, third, fourth or generation mode. One businessman told me he is so tired of hearing about word-processors that he is developing a bias against them.
We have to move above and beyond this level of thinking and begin to look at markets, market size, and market accessibility and ask how we are going to capture those markets. The Hon. gentleman for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) talked about the fish problem in Newfoundland. It is a serious problem. But there is an answer and a solution to it. I just wish we could take some of the marketing brains that I see in central Canada at whom he takes a kick once in a while and put them in Newfoundland. I want to tell the Hon. Member that there are ways to move that fish, but the way they are going about it, it will not be done. We have to determine how we are going to capture that market. Our products must be the best in the world, and we must look at that. The quality of the product one produces has to be second to none. If it is, you will sell it. I suggest to the Hon. Member that what is being produced now may not be the best there is. Excellence has to be our goal in production. Good value for our money must be our philosophy in trade. That is the area in which we have to move. If you adopted those principles in the marketing of fish
Supply
and you had the best possible product available packaged in an attractive way, and you aimed toward excellence and gave value for money, not the lowest price, not beating foreign competition, which devalues currency, I say to the Hon. Member he would have competition beating a path to his door to buy fish. I can assure the Hon. Member of that, because that philosophy works in all business, not just the fish industry.
I get tired of the bureaucratic games that are played with fiscal and tax policy. The bureaucrat seizes on a policy and his main concern is that a sum of money is moved equal to that set forward in the Budget document. Some of them, I think, would rather have half a dozen megaprojects going consuming several billion dollars than 400 projects that consume several hundred million dollars. A judgment error on megaprojects can spell disaster to an industry sector. We only need to look at the National Energy Program as an example.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I may conclude because it is almost five o'clock. If I do not, I will get into another area which will seem irrelevant to Hansard. May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
